x: Every new player is handed one: deer and their genes, troughs, woodland folk, farming, the kitchen garden, rivers, livestock, and the fairs and festivals.
Shy herds of the woods and meadows. Walk up openly and they flag their white tails and bolt. Sneak, or hold out apples or berries, and they let you near.

Every deer carries genes from both parents. A fawn is a blend of the two, give or take a little, so over the generations you can breed a herd towards what you want. Hold apples or berries and look at a deer to read it:
Five shades, light tan to dark chocolate. A fawn's coat falls between its parents'. In winter every coat turns greyer and thicker.
A stag's rack runs from a single spike to ten points, and bigger with every step. Does carry the gene too, and pass it on. Antlers are shed in winter and regrow through spring.
From small (85%) to huge (115%). A large deer gives an extra venison, a huge one two.

How close a deer lets you come before it bolts: Skittish: notices you 20 blocks off, bolts at 11. Wary: somewhere between. Calm: notices you at 10, bolts only at 4. Wild deer are mostly skittish. Breed calm ones together
Three rare coats run in families: Wild odds: piebald 1 in 50, melanistic 1 in 120, leucistic 1 in 200. Now and then a fawn gets a new copy, so no rare coat ever dies out.
Each deer has two copies of a rare gene, one from each parent. Two copies: it shows. One: a hidden carrier. P: a piebald copy. Two carriers: 1 fawn in 4 is piebald.
Carrier × carrier: 1 fawn in 4 shows it, 2 in 4 carry it. Shows × shows: every fawn shows it. Shows × carrier: half show it, the rest carry it. Carrier × clear: none show it, but half carry it.

Each gene is passed on by itself: breed a calm herd and a trophy line at the same time. Wild herds are families. Find one rare deer and its herdmates likely carry the gene too. Apples or berries put deer in the mood. A f
No deer can resist a heartberry cake: one of every wild berry. Feed it to a grown deer and it's yours. A tame deer fears no one. Another cake heals it.
Put a deer saddle on your tame deer and ride. Hold jump to gather a leap: a deer bounds higher and further than any horse. Deer land lightly. Shears take the saddle off.
Planks and an iron ingot make a small trough: Two small troughs make a trough; add one more for a long one. Each block holds 16 of one food.
Right-click with food to tip in a handful, or open it empty-handed to fill it and scoop some back. Animals come and eat what they would take from your hand:

Every trough meal adds a point; a day without one takes one away. Lean ○○○  no bonus Fed ●○○  +1 meat Well fed ●●○  +2 meat Prime ●●●  +3 meat Fattened animals fill out and look plumper. It takes about half an hour of st
Hold food an animal eats and look at it to see how it is doing: A meal also heals, helps the young grow, and starts breeding, unless 12 or more of their kind are already close by.
Tusked pigs of the deep woods. Come within 10 blocks and they charge; hurt a piglet and the whole sounder comes for you.

Hold an apple or a carrot and they calm down and follow it. Feed one: smoke means not yet, hearts mean it is yours (about 1 time in 3). A tame boar follows you, sits when you right-click it, guards you and breeds. Its pi

Go quietly in the woods and you'll meet porcupines, badgers by night, and chipmunks everywhere. Reindeer roam the snowy plains; and in the old woods, the elves. Creep (sneak) and most will let you near.
Herds of the snowy plains, and the deer's cousins: the same genes, bred the same way, tamed with a heartberry cake.

In snow they paw a crater for the lichen beneath. Lichen and moss bring them to you. As they walk, their knees click. Cows carry antlers too, smaller ones, and keep them through the winter; bulls cast theirs as winter be
Five shades from cream to dark, paler and shaggier in winter. Calves are a soft red-brown.
Hidden in the herd as with deer: dark, piebald, and the pure white reindeer every herder hopes for.
A tame reindeer takes its own harness: blanket, saddle, and a collar of brass bells. Then ride. Reindeer hide also tans to leather.
Slow, round and peaceable, until bothered. Stride up and the quills go up: it turns its back and pricks whatever touches it. Creep, and it won't mind.
Porcupines shed a quill now and then, and leave a few in anything that bothers them. A quill fletches arrows as well as a feather. They gnaw bark off logs, and love an apple.
Asleep by day, curled nose to tail; abroad at night, snuffling and digging for worms.
Crowd one and it bristles and grumbles: stay, and it bites. Leave it be. Its digging turns up worms, and now and then a root or a bone. Earthworms are what it loves: two well fed make cubs.
Always busy: it gathers seeds, nuts and berries until its cheeks bulge, then buries the lot.
Offer a chipmunk acorns: in time it trusts you, and brings you what it gathers. And a forgotten acorn comes up an oak. Acorns fall from oak leaves now and then; plant one yourself.
Shy folk of the old woods, in small bands, each with its glade. At dusk they dance there in a ring, and one plays the pipe.
Run at them and they're gone. Creep near and they'll bow. You cannot hurt an elf. They love sweet things: honey, flowers, berries, cake.

Give an elf a gift and it gives you its leaf-wrapped honey bread; one gift a day each. After that the band knows you. Now and then, to a friend, an elf gives its own pipe: play it, and the beasts come to listen.

Reindeer: the snowy plains, and nowhere else. Porcupines: woods and taiga. Badgers: woods, meadows and plains, at night. Chipmunks: woods and taiga, by day. Elves: flower woods, birch woods and dark woods. Look at dusk,

Farmland has a fertility from 0 to 10; fresh farmland is 6. Every harvest takes some out, and the same crop again and again takes more each time. Poor soil grows slowly; rich soil fast, and it gives a bigger harvest. Hol
Each harvest takes from the soil: So rotate: follow hungry crops with beans. Soil left resting regains a point a day, up to 8.
Fill a compost bin with garden waste. Full, it rots for half a day; turning it hurries it on: Compost feeds soil +3, manure +2. Trough-fed animals leave manure; it rots in the bin too.
Out of season crops grow slowly; glass keeps the seasons off.
Summer sun dries open fields. Sneak with a shovel on dirt to dig a ditch: it carries water 8 along to the fields. Fill the can at water; each use soaks 3x3.
On fine days crows raid fields of ripening crops, pecking them back. Walk out and they fly. No crow lands within 8 blocks of a scarecrow. Give it a carved pumpkin for a head.

Apple, pear, plum, cherry, peach and orange trees grow wild, each where it likes: oranges and peaches where it's warm. Their leaves drop saplings now and then. Plant one in the sun, or hurry it with bone meal.
Apple trees come in many kinds. Each has its own sapling, and its leaves drop saplings of the same kind. Wild apple trees can be any kind: look out for them in meadows and woods.
Red, Granny Smith, Golden Delicious, Cox's Orange Pippin, Russet; Crab, Bramley, Arkansas Black, Pink Pearl. Just for looks: every kind bears ordinary apples.

Right-click a leaf hung with ripe fruit to pick it. Cherries ripen first, oranges last: through the winter. Unpicked fruit withers at season's end. A picked leaf rests till it blossoms again. Deer love apples: hold one a

Blossom only turns to fruit if it's pollinated. Bees fly to trees in bloom; with a hive near the orchard, every flower sets. Without bees, wind and wild insects pollinate only about half. Keep a beehive within 16 blocks

Fruit in the press is squeezed into its vat: three fruit a bottle (six cherries), four bottles at most. Stand a long glass bottle under the spout and it fills. Apple, pear or haskap juice left a day turns to cider, perry

Break tall grass and now and then you'll find seeds for the garden: corn, tomatoes, squash and cabbage, and onions and garlic to plant as they are. Wild strawberries grow in meadows, plains, forests and cherry groves.
Grows two blocks tall, so leave it room. Ripe when the tassels turn gold; break either half for 1 to 3 cobs. Roast the cobs, or pop the kernels into popcorn.
They stop half-grown until you give them a garden stake to climb. Pick ripe ones with a right-click; they fruit again.

Once grown, a squash plant sends vines snaking out over open grass, up to ten blocks. Vines flower, and with bees about every flower sets a squash. Right-click ripe ones. The first frost kills the vines, dropping any rip
Onions, garlic and cabbages are hardy: they keep growing through winter, when other crops wait for spring. Plant an onion or a garlic clove as it is.

Turnips like the cold and grow on slowly through winter; sweet potatoes and chillies want warmth and rest in winter. Seeds come from their produce, slips from a sweet potato, and now and then from grass.
Turnips grow on in winter; sweet potatoes and chillies need glass. Ripe: a fat purple-topped root, tubers in the soil, red pods.
Roast turnips (and beetroot), bake sweet potatoes, dry chillies. Mash and stew give Warmth.
Low, leafy plants for grass or farmland. They flower in late spring and fruit into summer: right-click to pick. From midsummer they send out runners that root new plants close by.
Onions and cabbages grow on through winter as well.
Soups and stews from the garden fill you up and give you Warmth. While Warmth lasts the winter cold can't get at you, and you thaw out as if by a fire. A stew lasts longest.
Craft a corn cob into 3 kernels, a tomato into 2 seeds and a squash into 4 seeds to sow again. Strawberries look after themselves, spreading by runners.

Left standing when ripe, a plant goes to seed. Harvest it then for seed with its genes (and fewer crops). An ordinary harvest gives back the seed you sowed. Hold seed and look at a plant to read its genes. A tin compares
Save from your best. Corn, squash and cabbage cross with neighbours; bees carry it further. Settled lines earn names.
Garlic bread, cornbread, popcorn, coleslaw, strawberries and cream, and strawberry jam. Look them up in your recipe book.
Crafted in any order, with a bowl.
Low bushes carpeting northern woods, heaths and meadows. Pick the dusty blue berries all summer; they ripen again. White bells in spring, blazing red in autumn. Bushes spread slowly.
A hardy shrub of the cold north, two blocks tall. Its long blue berries are the first fruit of the year. Pale yellow flowers at winter's end, ripe in late spring, gold in autumn.
Ankle-high in bogs, swamps and snowy tundra. Each stem holds one berry: hard and red at first, soft and gold when ripe. White flowers in late spring, ripe in high summer. Spreads into bog patches.
A low evergreen under the pines. Tart red berries ripen in autumn and hang on under the snow. Pink bells in spring; leaves bronze in winter but never fall.
Canes two blocks tall at the edges of broadleaf woods. Soft red berries in high summer; new canes come up around them. Yellow leaves in autumn, bare brown canes in winter.
A thorny bramble that creeps outwards. It snags and scratches whoever pushes through. Black berries from late summer. Ripens unevenly: red and black berries together. Foxes slip through unharmed.

A tall shrub of woods and hedges. In early summer, pick its cream flower plates for elderflowers, or leave them for berries. You can't have both: a picked elder has no berries that year. Raw elderberries upset the stomac
A thorny, silver-leaved shrub of beaches and stony shores. Its branches are packed with orange berries from autumn into winter. Grows in sand and gravel. Press the berries for juice.
Press berries for juice. Haskap juice left a day turns to haskap wine.
Any wild berry makes jam: a bottle, three berries and sugar. Crumble and forager's mix take any wild berries.
Cordial puts a spring in your step; syrup warms you through. Press raspberries or sea buckthorn too.

In forest and taiga: reishi, lion's mane and turkey tail on trunks, chaga on birch, shiitake on fallen logs, maitake at tree roots. Break one to pick it; replant it where it grows. Maitake also comes up under trees in au
Two of one mushroom, a glass bottle and a honey bottle make a tincture. Reishi: Regeneration. Lion's mane: Haste. Turkey tail: cures Poison.
Chaga: Resistance. Shiitake: Absorption. Maitake: Speed. Drink one even when full; the bottle comes back.
Forest stew gives Warmth.
Gnomes, bird baths and more are made at a Tinker's Bench, which shows what each piece takes. Pick one, press Make. Shift makes up to eight.
Dye a gnome's hat to change it. They move at night, they say. Birds visit the bath on fine days; the weathervane turns into the wind; the sundial tells the time.
Plank frames full of rich soil. Crops grow as on farmland and nothing tramples them. Beds side by side join up. Water one end and it spreads. Summer dries beds fast; winter never.
Bury a clay olla in a bed and fill it with a bucket: it keeps the soil round it moist for days. Wheat or hay on a bed is mulch: it dries half as fast.
Dig with a spade and now and then a worm turns up, more after rain. Put some in a wormery. Feed it greens (scraps) and browns (paper, leaves, straw) evenly, or it sours or dries.

Castings: +5 fertility, +2 round about. The best soil food there is. Worm tea from the tap: pour it on a bed to feed the soil and lift the crops. Happy worms multiply. Bring the bin in for a hard winter. A worm on you is
What bites depends on the water (rapids, river, lake, swamp or sea), the season and the hour. Each fish is weighed as you land it.
Trout and grayling love the rapids; trout bite best at dawn and dusk. Eels feed by night. In autumn the salmon run up the rivers.
Perch bite by day, pike at dawn and dusk, carp all summer. Catfish lurk in warm swamps at night. In the frozen north, Arctic char live under the ice: break a hole and fish through it.
Brown Trout · not yet Grayling · not yet Perch · not yet Pike · not yet Carp · not yet Eel · not yet Catfish · not yet Arctic Char · not yet Blind Cave Fish · not yet
Raw Salmon · not yet Raw Cod · not yet Pufferfish · not yet Tropical Fish · not yet Your heaviest of each, and how many you've landed.
Cook any fish, then smoke it in a smoker, bake it into fish pie, or cook trout with garlic and onion.
Look into a river: trout, grayling and char hold their place in the current, facing upstream, darting off after a fly now and then. Pike lie still in wait.
Use a water bucket on a river fish to carry it home; the bucket says which fish is inside. Let it go in a pond of your own.
Cows, pigs and chickens pass on genes like deer: a blend of both parents. Size (more meat), growth (young grow faster) and fertility (shorter rest, twins).
Hens: laying. The best lay eggs half as often again. Pigs: litters. Twins up to half the time, and triplets. Cows: hide. Thick-hided cows give extra leather.
A book and a sapling make this Field Guide; the breed books need leather, a porkchop or a feather.
Hang a wall bookshelf to keep your books; an egg carton holds 16 eggs.
Once a year Judge Bramblewick, an old badger in tweed, comes to every show bench. Last day of autumn: judging at noon.
Set a show bench up on your farm and open it to set out your entries. Fences near the bench get bunting on fair morning.
On the bench: mead, honey, preserves, eggs, a fruit basket, and the heaviest vegetable. Each is marked out of a hundred against the villagers' best. Hover a class to see what wins.
Tie your best cow, pig and bird to a fence near the bench. Fattening, size and breeding count. A brushed animal shows better.
Rosettes for first, second and third; a silver cup for the best of all. Each prize earns fair points. The villagers try harder every time you win.
Spend fair points at the prize table: from the bench, or ask the judge. Bunting, rare seeds, a show brush, giant pumpkin seeds, a fairy lantern, Buckfast bees.
A giant pumpkin grows all summer on rich, wet farmland, and drinks the soil dry. Keep it composted and watered. Break it to weigh it.
Hang it above a fence line or across a lane, and every day's a fair day. It strings itself the way you're facing.
The middle day of summer. Build a bonfire: at dusk it lights itself, and the village dances round it till dawn. Leap the flames on Midsummer Eve for a year's luck.
Five flowers woven into a crown, worn on the head. Petals drift about whoever wears one. Any small flowers will do.
Nine breeds of cattle, dairy, beef and dual-purpose, and how to breed for the traits you want.
Dairy The great black-and-white milker: fertile, and ready to milk again in a minute. Milk again: 1 min. Horns: mostly polled.
Dairy Small, fawn and gentle, with short horns and a dark face. A fine little dairy cow. Milk again: 1½ min. Horns: short.
Dairy Golden with white patches and short horns. A steady, fertile dairy cow. Milk again: 1½ min. Horns: short.
Kept for milk: ready to milk again soonest. Keep one bull, and milk the cows in turn.
Beef Solid black and hornless. Grows fast and big: the beef breed. Milk again: 5 min. Horns: mostly polled.
Beef Red with a white face and spreading horns. Big for beef, with a thick hide. Milk again: 5 min. Horns: medium.
Beef Grey, with a hump, a dewlap and long ears. Hardy, with more health, and common in hot lands. Milk again: 4 min. Horns: stubby.
Kept for meat: big, fast-growing, slow to milk. Fatten them at a trough for the most meat.
Dual-purpose Gold-red with a white face and patches. Good for both milk and beef. Milk again: 2½ min. Horns: short.
Dual-purpose Red roan with long horns. Dual-purpose, with a good thick hide. Milk again: 2½ min. Horns: long.
Dual-purpose Big, gentle and light red, without horns. Dual-purpose and large. Milk again: 3 min. Horns: mostly polled.
A bit of both: good size and middling milk. A good first herd: milk now, beef later.
Nine breeds of pig, from prolific Yorkshires to heritage Tamworths.
Prolific The big pink pig: very fertile and fast growing. The classic farm pig. Litters: medium. Growth: big.
Prolific · Feed-efficient Long body, ears over its eyes. Feed-efficient: each trough meal counts double. Litters: medium. Growth: medium.
Prolific White, with hanging ears. A good mother, with the biggest litters. Litters: big. Growth: medium.
Bred for big litters and quick growth. Start a herd with these: it soon grows.
Meaty Red-brown and fast growing, with good meat on it. Litters: medium. Growth: big.
Meaty · Hardy Black with a white belt over its shoulders. Hardy, with more health. Litters: medium. Growth: medium.
Meaty Pale with black spots, and very muscular: the biggest for meat. Litters: small. Growth: medium.
Bred for size and meat. Fatten them at a trough for the most pork.
Heritage · Flavourful Black with white feet, face and tail tip. Flavourful: an extra chop. Litters: medium. Growth: medium.
Heritage · Forager Ginger, with a long snout. A forager: it fattens itself grazing on grass. Litters: medium. Growth: medium.
Heritage · Hybrid vigour Black with white points and hanging ears. Its crossbred piglets grow faster. Litters: medium. Growth: big.
Old breeds, each with a gift. Cross a Poland China with others for fast-growing piglets.
Fifteen breeds of chicken, the eggs they lay, and four kinds of quail.
Egg layer White and light, with a big red comb. The best layer of all: eggs nearly every day. Eggs: many, white. Size: few.
Egg layer A friendly brown hybrid, bred on farms for steady laying. Eggs: many, brown. Size: some.
Egg layer Lavender-blue, with a fluffy beard and cheek muffs. It lays sky-blue eggs. Eggs: many, blue. Size: some.
Egg layer Black with copper hackles. It lays the darkest eggs of all: deep chocolate brown. Eggs: many, chocolate. Size: some.
Light birds bred to lay and lay. The best hens lay half as often again: hold seeds and look at one.
Each breed lays its own colour: white, cream, brown, sky blue or chocolate. A thrown egg hatches a breed that lays that colour. An egg carton (five paper) holds 16 eggs of any colour in one slot.
Meat bird Broad and muscled, it grows the fastest: the meat bird. Eggs: few, brown. Size: many.
Meat bird A gentle giant with feathered feet and a soft, fluffy coat. Eggs: some, brown. Size: many.
Meat bird Black and green-sheened, the biggest chicken of them all. Eggs: some, brown. Size: many.
Heavy birds bred for size. They lay less, but grow big and fast.
Dual-purpose Deep red-brown and tough. A good layer and a good table bird. Eggs: many, brown. Size: some.
Dual-purpose White with a black-flecked collar and tail: an old English all-rounder. Eggs: many, cream. Size: some.
Dual-purpose Barred black and white all over. Hardy, calm and productive. Eggs: many, brown. Size: some.
Dual-purpose Glossy black with a green sheen: the best layer of the all-rounders. Eggs: many, brown. Size: some.
A good egg and a good roast. The easiest first flock for a new farm.
One rooster is enough for a run of hens. Mixed breeds cross happily, and chicks may favour either parent. Keep the rooster with the hens: a Silkie needs one near to hatch chicks.
Ornamental · Broody Fluffy as fur, with a pom-pom crest and feathered feet. A broody hen. Eggs: few, cream. Size: few.
Ornamental · Fine feathers A huge pom-pom crest over its eyes, and fine feathers. Eggs: few, white. Size: few.
Ornamental · Fine feathers A tiny bantam with every feather laced in black. Eggs: few, cream. Size: few.
Ornamental · Fine feathers A big ball of feathers down to its toes, and a fine moult. Eggs: few, brown. Size: many.
Kept for looks, and their gifts. Small, but a Silkie hatches her own chicks.

Broody (Silkie): with a rooster nearby, some of her eggs hatch at once into chicks. Fine feathers (Polish, Sebright, Cochin): they moult a feather now and then. A coop of fancy hens keeps you in feathers for arrows and q
The brown barred farm quail of meadows and fields. The best layer: an egg every couple of minutes.
Chestnut, with a white throat and eye stripe. The wild quail of plains and field edges.
Blue-grey with a black face and a curling plume. Lives in savanna and scrub.
The tiniest quail, slate-blue and chestnut. Hides in jungle and warm grassland.

Quails live in small coveys. They eat seeds like chickens, breed with seeds, and lay speckled quail eggs. They are flighty: walk up openly and they scurry off. Sneak, or hold seeds, to get close. A fall never hurts them:
Quail eggs bake like any egg and fit a carton; thrown, one may hatch. Their barred feathers fletch arrows. Cook raw quail in a furnace, smoker or on a campfire.
Bees and their kinds, skeps and frame hives, honeys from every flower, mead, and the herb garden.

A colony lives in its hive and flies out to work flowers up to twelve blocks away, bringing nectar home. What the honey becomes depends on what they work: plant for it. Rain and winter keep them in. A hive with nothing i

Wild colonies nest in birch and oak, most of all in flower forests, and in savanna acacias. The kind is the country's, and a nest's colour tells you whose it is. An empty skep takes a nest's bees home with you.
The everyday bee of meadows and woods. Steady in every season, middling in temper. Wild in plains, forests and most temperate country. Plain golden nests.

The old dark bee of the north. Works through grey, cool weather and even a little in winter, but never makes much. Wild in the taiga and snowy country, in dark brown nests. Short-tempered: always smoke them.
Golden, gentle and the great honey-maker, but a hungry colony that eats its capped frames in winter. Wild in the savanna, nesting in acacias. Amber nests.
Grey and gentle bees of the mountains. The quickest of all to build up in spring. Wild in meadows, cherry groves and the hills. Grey-green nests.
A cross of Italian and Carniolan: gentle, hard-working, and easy to keep. Never found wild: see Breeding Buckfasts.
Woken out of amber, a bee lost for ages. Works steadily from early spring until the cold, and a little even in winter. Never found wild: only in amber, deep under old forests. Middling temper.

Seams of amber run in the rock under old forests. Once in a while a lump holds a bee, caught long ago. Hold it with an empty skep and it wakes: an ancient bee. Mine amber without silk touch, or you'll only get the seam.
How hard each works through the year, and its temper. Click a bee to turn to its page.
Hold an empty skep to a wild bee nest and use it: the bees come with it, of whatever kind lives there. A skep of bees can be carried and set down anywhere.
Straw, simple and old. When it's full, take honey with a bottle or comb with shears, like any hive. A skep has no frames: for named honeys you need a frame hive.
Put empty frames in (up to eight). As the hive fills, the bees draw them out and cap them with honey.
A sheet of paper in a frame of sticks. The bees build comb on it, fill it, and cap it with wax. No frames, no honey of its own: keep a few spare in.
Use a skep of bees on a frame hive to tip the colony in. The bees take the skep's kind with them.
Open a hive with an empty hand to look in: its bees, its frames, and what they're working. Lift capped frames out on its screen; smoke them first.
Smoke calms bees. Work with a campfire under the hive, a smoker in either hand, or Beekeeper's Calm. Without it, a colony may boil out and sting.

In spring a crowded colony sends half its bees off with the old queen. They hang in a buzzing cluster under a branch nearby. Hold an empty skep to it to catch it. Left alone, in a couple of days it moves into an empty hi
Keep Italian and Carniolan colonies within twenty-four blocks of each other. A swarm from either may come out Buckfast. Catch it and you have the gentlest, hardest-working bees of all.

Spring: colonies build up; fruit blossom and berry flowers. Summer: the main flow. Frames fill fast. Autumn: the flow slows; honeydew in the pines. Winter: clustered and still. Leave Italians something to eat.

Each frame fills with whatever the bees worked most while filling it. If one source is close to half of it all, the honey is named for it. Otherwise it's wildflower. An orchard in blossom, a field of sunflowers, a lavend
Put capped frames in the extractor, turn the crank, and draw the honey off into bottles. A frame gives three jars, wax and the frame back. Effects last three minutes.
Golden and mixed, from a meadow of everything. Forager's Eye: ripe fruit, berries and crops nearby sparkle From: Any flowers, when no one kind leads.
Pale and delicate, from apple, pear, plum and peach blossom. Beekeeper's Calm: bees won't stay angry at you From: Fruit trees in blossom, in spring.
Bright and perfumed, from orange trees in flower. Vigour: you tire half as fast From: Orange trees in blossom, where it's warm.
Faintly pink, from cherry blossom. Petal Fall: you fall softly From: Cherry trees and cherry groves, in spring.
Dark and fruity, from the flowers of berry bushes. Green Thumb: plants you walk among grow on From: Blueberry, raspberry, bramble and more in flower.
Thick and sunny yellow. Sunlit: out in the sun, you slowly fill up From: Fields of sunflowers, all summer.
Pale violet, and calming. Serenity: monsters notice you later From: Lavender, from the herb garden.
Dark, strong forest honey, not from flowers but the sweet dew on spruce. Rooted: hard to knock back From: Spruce woods, when little else flowers.
Rare, sea-green honey from flowers older than the world. Old Sight: monsters nearby glow From: Torchflowers and pitcher plants.
Click a honey to turn to its page.
Honey and water left to work in an oak barrel, and aged in a cool cellar until it's mellow and strong. The barrel is two blocks long; its tap faces you.

Use honey jars, water buckets and up to three additions on the open barrel. Two jars to each bucket at least. Press the wax seal on its screen (or crouch and use it) to seal it. Up to six jars and two buckets: three bott
Every mead keeps its honey's effect too.

Cook a jar of honey in a furnace until it's dark and bitter-sweet: caramelised honey makes a bochet. Wheat in the must makes a braggot, half mead and half ale. A smoker or campfire caramelises honey too.
Mead is drinkable after three days, and better the longer it's kept, up to vintage. A vintage's own effect is stronger too. Use the barrel to see how it's coming on.

A barrel ages only where it's cool: no sky above, nothing hot nearby, and dug down below the surface (or in cold country). Warm, it stops ageing; warm two days altogether and it sours. Sour mead draws off as honey vinega
Sweet berries and glow berries work too.

Use a glass bottle on the barrel to draw a bottle of mead from the tap. Each bottle is named for what it is: a Fine Raspberry Melomel, a Vintage Lavender Sack Mead. Young mead can be rough: let it age.
Lavender grows in warm open country, chamomile in meadows, mint by water and nettles in the woods. Pick and plant them anywhere; a bed slowly spreads. Nettles sting bare legs: wear boots.

A glass bottle and two sprigs make a tea. Herbs in the barrel make a metheglin with the herb's touch. Lavender: Serenity. Chamomile: Regeneration. Mint: Water Breathing. Nettle: Resistance. Bees working lavender make lav
Crop genetics: pollination, saving seed, and breeding better varieties.
Each runs from 0 to 15. An ordinary plant is about 7 or 8.
Every gene comes in two copies, one from each parent. The plant shows the average of the two. This plant looks ordinary, yet carries a fine copy it can pass on.

The bars show what its seedlings will show, on average. Gen counts how often the line has been saved. Breeds true: five dots and every seedling comes out alike. Fewer, and they scatter. Hover over a packet to read it.
Hold any seed and look at a crop: its genes show above your hotbar. It says too whether the plant has gone to seed. Walk your rows before harvest and note your best.
Each seed takes one copy of every gene from its mother, and one from the father whose pollen set it, by chance. Each square is one chance in four.
Wheat, beans, tomatoes and chillies pollinate themselves. A neighbour's pollen gets in only now and then. Their lines stay pure easily.
The wind crosses corn and beetroot: nearly every plant takes a neighbour's pollen. Insects cross these, about half the time; with bees near, nearly always.
Pollen travels this many blocks. Grow lines further apart to keep them pure.

Potatoes, garlic and sweet potatoes grow from the plant itself: the same plant again. Now and then a clone sports: one gene shifts on its own. A potato left to go to seed gives true seed you can cross.
Bees, or a hive within 16 blocks, carry pollen two blocks further and far more often. For pure seed, keep insect-crossed lines away from the hives.

Leave a ripe plant standing most of a day and it goes to seed: fluff drifts from it. Harvest it then for saved seed: its own genes and its pollen father's. More seed, less crop. Saved seed may not breed true.
Pick a ripe plant before it goes to seed and you get its crop, and the packet you sowed back, unchanged. So a field sown from one packet gives back seed that stacks.
Save from your best plants and the line creeps up each year. Save from the worst and it slides back. Look over each plant before harvest, or compare packets in a tin. Only the best few go to seed.
Holds nine packets side by side, a bar chart under each. Gold marks the best. Keep one tin for each crop.
Each year, save seed only from the best few plants. Slow and steady: about a step a year.
Two different copies and the seedlings scatter. Two matched copies pass on every time. Save a line from itself a few years and it settles, and earns a name.
Cross two settled lines and every seedling gets one copy from each: an even first generation. A first cross grows strongly: hybrid vigour.
Save seed from that cross and the copies shuffle again: some take after one grandparent, some the other. Here are the surprises. Pick the best and start a new line.
Plants with mixed copies grow stronger. Crops that cross freely gain most from it. Inbred too long, those same crops grow weak. Selfers like wheat hardly mind inbreeding.

About one copy in 25 shifts a step as seed is made; now and then, two or three. Once in about 120 savings a sport appears: one trait leaps, and the line becomes a named heirloom. The fair and the pedlar give heirlooms to
Yield sets the harvest: from 0.6 to 1.4 times an ordinary plant's. Weak plants dawdle; vigorous ones grow up to a third faster.
Hardy plants bear dry soil and the wrong season better. The hardiest grow on through winter now and then, and shrug off killing frost. Breed it for early and late sowing.
Their average grades the produce: Ordinary produce isn't graded.
Graded produce scores in the fruit and veg basket: 3 marks a grade. A giant pumpkin's size gene sets how fast it swells: half to half again as fast. Save seed from your champion.
1. Sow common carrot seed in a bed. 2. Look over each plant; note the biggest and tastiest. 3. Let only those go to seed, near your hives.
4. Sow their seed in a bed of its own, well apart. 5. Save from the best again, every year. 6. In three or four years it breeds true, and takes a name. Then cross it with an heirloom.
Keep a seed tin for each crop. Name a fine line at an anvil. Raised beds keep lines apart. A clone keeps a perfect plant for good.
What waits underground: wonders, folk, finds, the root cellar and the kit to carry.
Some cave roofs are hung with glow-worm silk, beaded with soft blue light. Run about and they go dark; keep quiet and they come back. Shear silk for a lantern: bottle, silk, stick.
Pools of warm water deep down. A soak warms you right through. Drop in herbs or honey for an herbal bath:
Pale crystal glowing in deep hollows. Brush past and each rings its own note. Their shards make wind chimes.
Long dark rivers wind through the rock, deep enough for a boat, with a ledge to walk on. Blind cave fish bite there.
Old figures in ochre on the walls. Put paper to one to take a rubbing. Eight figures to find.
Seams under old forests. Now and then a lump holds a bee or a seed. Four amber make a glowing block.
Walk a pig on a lead in oak or birch woods: now and then it roots one up. Tamworths have the best noses.
Out in damp caves, and in the woods in rain. Cabbage tempts them; pick one up by hand. Cook one for escargot.
A log plugged with spawn fruits in the dark and damp: a cellar, or a cave by water. Lion's mane works too. Pick by hand.
Roots and apples kept three days in a crate somewhere cool and dark come out cellar-sweet. More filling than fresh.
A mead barrel deep in a cave ages half again as fast: the cold there is steady all year. The barrel says 'Cave cellar'.
In winter, in cold country, icicles grow on the roofs of caves near the surface. They melt in spring. Silk touch keeps one.
Blow it and the echo outlines the caves round you. Gold rings mean a way out. Good when you're lost.
Glow-worm lanterns light without smoke. A hot spring cures the winter chill. Keep gold nuggets for the new moon. Leave the knockers something nice.
